title: Nozick, Sen and the Capability Approach

cards.b:
Rawls offered one answer to the question "what is a just distribution?" Two powerful replies came from opposite sides.

Robert Nozick, Rawls's Harvard colleague, said Rawls gave the state far too much power. Justice is about respecting rights, not engineering outcomes. He stands for libertarianism.

Amartya Sen, the Indian economist and Nobel laureate (1998), said Rawls focused on the wrong thing. What matters is not the resources people have, but what they can actually do and be. He built the capability approach, developed further by Martha Nussbaum.

UPSC asks about each thinker and about comparisons with Rawls.

Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) opens boldly: "Individuals have rights, and there are things no person or group may do to them (without violating their rights)."

The base is self-ownership. You own your body, your talents and your labour. This draws on Locke, and on Kant's idea that people must be treated as ends, never merely as means.

Rights are side constraints. They are not goals to maximise but limits on what anyone may do. You may not violate one person's rights even to prevent more violations elsewhere.

So the state's job is narrow: protection against force, theft and fraud, and enforcement of contracts. This is the minimal state.

Nozick's theory of justice in holdings has three parts:

  1. Justice in acquisition: how unowned things first become owned. He uses a version of Locke's proviso: acquisition is fine if it doesn't worsen others' situation.
  2. Justice in transfer: things pass justly by voluntary exchange, gift or inheritance.
  3. Rectification: correcting past injustices in acquisition or transfer, such as theft or conquest.

If you got your holdings justly, you are entitled to them. Full stop.

So justice is historical: it depends on how a distribution came about. Rawls's theory, by contrast, is patterned and end-state: it judges the final distribution by a pattern, such as "benefit the worst-off".

Nozick's most famous argument uses the basketball star Wilt Chamberlain.

Start with any distribution you think is just, say perfect equality. Now a million fans each happily pay 25 cents extra to watch Wilt play. At season's end, Wilt has $250,000, far more than anyone else.

Is the new distribution unjust? Everyone chose freely. No one was harmed.

Nozick's point: liberty upsets patterns. To keep any pattern, the state would have to keep interfering in free exchanges.

He concludes that taxation of earnings from labour is on a par with forced labour. It forces you to work some hours for others' purposes.

Nozick also argued that a minimal state could arise from anarchy without violating rights, through private protective agencies. The book's last part offers a framework for utopia: many voluntary communities under one minimal state.

• Weak foundations: Thomas Nagel, in "Libertarianism without Foundations" (1975), said Nozick asserts rights without proving them.
  • Rectification: almost all property today traces back to conquest, slavery or fraud. Taken seriously, rectification could justify huge redistribution. Nozick himself admitted this.
  • Self-ownership: G.A. Cohen, in Self-Ownership, Freedom, and Equality (1995), argued that full self-ownership produces unacceptable inequality and unfreedom for the poor.
  • Freedom for whom? Formal freedom to trade means little to someone with nothing to trade.
  • Nozick himself later wrote, in The Examined Life (1989), that his libertarian position now seemed "seriously inadequate".

In his 1979 Tanner Lecture, "Equality of What?", Sen asked a simple question. When we say people should be equal, equal in what?

  • Utility (happiness)? But people adapt to hardship. A deprived person may learn to want little and report being content. Sen calls this adaptive preference.
  • Primary goods (Rawls)? But people differ in how they convert resources into well-being. A disabled person needs more resources to move around than others. A pregnant woman needs more food.

Sen's answer: we should focus on capabilities, the real freedoms people have to achieve things they value.

Functionings are the things a person actually does or is: being well-fed, healthy, literate, taking part in community life.

Capabilities are the set of functionings a person could achieve: their real freedom to choose.

Sen's example: a person who fasts and a person who starves both lack food. But the faster has the capability to eat and chooses not to. The starving person has no choice. Justice cares about that difference.

cards.h: Development as Freedom and The Idea of Justice
cards.b:
Development as Freedom (1999)

Development is the expansion of real freedoms, not just GDP growth. Sen names five instrumental freedoms: political freedoms, economic facilities, social opportunities, transparency guarantees and protective security.

Famines and democracy

In Poverty and Famines (1981), Sen showed famines come from a collapse of people's entitlements, not just a shortage of food. He studied the Bengal famine of 1943. He later argued that no major famine has occurred in a functioning democracy with a free press.

The Idea of Justice (2009)

Sen rejects Rawls's search for a perfectly just society. He calls it transcendental institutionalism. Instead, he favours comparative justice: compare real options and remove manifest injustices. He uses the Indian ideas of niti (rules, institutions) and nyaya (realised justice in people's lives).

Sen refused to give a fixed list of capabilities. He said each society should decide through public reasoning.

Martha Nussbaum disagreed. In Women and Human Development (2000) and Creating Capabilities (2011), she gave a list of ten central human capabilities that every government should guarantee up to a threshold:

  1. Life
  2. Bodily health
  3. Bodily integrity
  4. Senses, imagination and thought
  5. Emotions
  6. Practical reason
  7. Affiliation
  8. Other species
  9. Play
  10. Control over one's environment, political and material

She drew on Aristotle's idea of flourishing and used fieldwork with poor women in India, including SEWA in Ahmedabad.

• Focus: Rawls looks at primary goods. Nozick looks at entitlements and how holdings arose. Sen looks at capabilities, what people can do and be.
  • State: Rawls supports a welfare state. Nozick wants a minimal state. Sen supports public action in health, education and social security, alongside markets.
  • Method: Rawls uses an ideal contract. Nozick reasons from rights. Sen compares real-world situations.

Critics of Sen say the capability approach is hard to measure and too open-ended. Critics of Nussbaum say her list imposes one idea of the good life on all cultures.

• The UNDP's Human Development Index (1990), created by Mahbub ul Haq with Sen, measures health, education and income, not just GDP.
  • NITI Aayog's National Multidimensional Poverty Index uses the global MPI method (developed by OPHI and UNDP, inspired by Sen). Its 2023 report said about 13.5 crore Indians left multidimensional poverty between 2015–16 and 2019–21.
  • Rights-based laws like MGNREGA (2005), the Right to Education (2009) and the National Food Security Act (2013) aim at capabilities.
  • Sen and Jean Drèze wrote An Uncertain Glory: India and Its Contradictions (2013), arguing India's growth neglected health and education.

On the libertarian side, the 1991 reforms drew on market arguments, though India never adopted a minimal state.

Structure for Nozick: self-ownership, side constraints, the three principles of entitlement, Wilt Chamberlain, minimal state, then Nagel's and Cohen's critiques.

Structure for Sen: "Equality of what?", functionings and capabilities (draw the diagram), fasting vs starving, niti and nyaya, Nussbaum's list. End with HDI, MPI and India's rights-based laws.
